problem: Prior VLN agents such as Speaker-Follower, Self-Monitoring, Regretful Agent, FAST and EnvDrop encode each instruction as one mixed representation. They then match that single representation jointly against the concatenated visual and orientation features of the candidate viewpoints. This entangles object descriptions ('the table') with action specifications ('turn left'), even though the two need to be grounded to different signals.
motivation: Action phrases mostly relate to the orientation of a candidate viewpoint and can decide the next move without visual perception. Object phrases correspond to visual appearance, not orientation. Mixing them may limit instruction–vision and instruction–orientation grounding. Separating them creates a side problem: the mentioned object may be visible from several candidates, so the agent drifts off the shortest path. That calls for a path-fidelity training signal.
key_idea: Decompose the progress-conditioned instruction attention into an object stream matched only to candidate visual features and an action stream matched only to candidate orientation features, fuse their scores with adaptively predicted weights, and train with a nearest-point path loss that penalizes steps away from the ground-truth path.
insight: The two components are complementary. On R2R val-unseen, OAAM alone gives only +1 SR (50→51) and leaves SPL unchanged at 47. NPL alone raises val-seen SPL (60→66) but hurts unseen SR (50→48). Together they give 54 SR / 50 SPL, because NPL keeps OAAM's object-driven choices on the ground-truth path. The module ablation shows the action/orientation stream generalizes much better than the object/visual stream: unseen SR is 44 with the AA stream alone versus 26 with the OA stream alone. The learned fusion weights average 0.82 for AA versus 0.18 for OA, consistent with visual features overfitting to seen environments. Still, the adaptive combination beats either stream alone by 10–28 SPL on val-unseen.
method: Base navigator (EnvDrop): Bi-LSTM encodes instruction words; an LSTM decoder takes attended panoramic ResNet features plus the previous action embedding; soft attention over words yields the instruction-aware state h̃_t. EnvDrop's back-translation speaker augmentation and environmental-dropout augmentation are reused.

Object-Aware (OA) module: separate word attention γ_t = softmax(u_j^T W_O h_t), conditioned on decoder state for progress; ũ_t^o feeds h̃_t^o = tanh(W_P[ũ_t^o; h_t]); candidate score G^OA = m_{t,k}^T W_H h̃_t^o uses ONLY the candidate's visual (ResNet) feature.

Action-Aware (AA) module: same structure with its own attention δ_t = softmax(u_j^T W_A h_t) and h̃_t^a = tanh(W_K[ũ_t^a; h_t]); candidate score G^AA = n_{t,k}^T W_F h̃_t^a uses ONLY the 4-d orientation feature (cos/sin heading, cos/sin elevation).

Adaptive combination module: per-step weight vector w_t = W_T ũ_t, predicted from the vision-aware attentive instruction feature; P(a_{t,k}) = softmax([G^OA; G^AA] w_t). The navigable viewpoint with max probability is chosen.

Nearest Point Loss (NPL): L^NP = Σ_t log p_t(a_t) · D_t^NP, where D_t^NP is the shortest-path distance from the agent's current viewpoint to the nearest viewpoint on the ground-truth path. This is zero on-path and grows with deviation. It differs from the CLS reward, which instead matches each GT-path viewpoint to its nearest trajectory point.
Training: EnvDrop two-stage schedule, first on real training data and then on speaker/env-dropout augmented data, with mixed IL + RL losses plus NPL. Inference is greedy argmax.

setting.backbone: EnvDrop-style Bi-LSTM instruction encoder + LSTM decoder with attention (trained from scratch) over pre-computed frozen ImageNet ResNet features
setting.training_data: R2R train split (14,025 instructions) plus EnvDrop augmented data: speaker back-translated (trajectory, instruction) pairs and environmental-dropout 'new' environments. For R4R, trained on the R4R train split, presumably with the same pipeline.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 discrete views, ResNet features) + per-candidate orientation features (heading/elevation sin/cos)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (select among navigable candidate viewpoints)
setting.privileged: none at test time (the ground-truth path is used only for the NPL training loss)

numbers_note: All metrics are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.54) and are converted here to 0-100. TL is in meters. The OA/AA module analysis text mentions Test-split results, but Table 2 only reports Val Seen and Val Unseen. NE is not reported. The R2R SDTW/CLS values for the main model come from ablation Table 1, since Table 3 omits them. The Baseline+NPL-only ablation row is omitted: it does not contain OAAM.
results: On R2R, OAAM+NPL reaches SPL 50 on both val-unseen (SR 54) and test (SR 53). This beats its EnvDrop baseline (SPL 47 on both) and FAST (SPL 44 / 41), although FAST has higher SR (56 / 54) at much longer trajectories (TL ~20–22 m). On R4R val-unseen it sets a new state of the art with CLS 40, versus 37 for PTA high-level and 34 for EnvDrop, while roughly halving EnvDrop's trajectory length (13.80 vs 26.97). On seen environments it ranks only about third, behind FAST and the Regretful Agent in R2R SPL.
limitations: It fits seen environments less well than FAST and the Regretful Agent (val-seen SPL 62 vs 64/63), which the authors attribute to under-exploiting training data.

Object/action separation is learned purely through soft attention with no explicit supervision. An NLTK-based check finds the OA module's top-3 words contain a noun only ~80% of the time, and the AA module's contain a verb ~75% of the time. The OA stream also contributes little (mean weight 0.18) and generalizes poorly.
Gains depend on the OAAM+NPL combination: NPL alone hurts unseen SR, and OAAM alone does not improve unseen SPL. Absolute R4R success remains low (SR 31, SDTW 11 unseen).
